opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus Christ speaks a difficult truth: “No prophet is accepted in his own native place.” To make the point, He reaches back to the time of Elisha.

In those days Israel had grown spiritually compromised. Yet one of Elisha’s most striking miracles was not given to an Israelite. It was given to Naaman, a Syrian commander from a nation often hostile to Israel. Naaman expected a dramatic cure for his leprosy, but Elisha sent only a simple command: wash seven times in the Jordan. When Naaman humbled himself and obeyed, he was healed. The outsider trusted the prophet’s word and received life.

The people of Nazareth understood the implication. Just as Israel once resisted the prophets, they were now resisting the one standing before them. Admiration quickly turned to fury. They drove Jesus out of town and toward the edge of the hill intending to throw Him down. Yet the Gospel records a striking calm:

“But he passed through the midst of them and went away.”
(Gospel of Luke 4:30)

They could not stop Him. His hour had not yet come.

Later, when the time arrived, Jesus did not slip away. He went to Jerusalem willingly and openly, accepting the Cross.

What began in Nazareth revealed a pattern that would unfold again and again: some who believed they already knew God rejected Him, while many outsiders received Him with humility and faith. The same invitation stands for us today. We must set aside the divisions that separate us and unite under Christ, who continues to offer Himself freely to all hearts willing to receive Him.
